Editorial

Anne Hurley and Teresa Bailey

Teresa Bailey

Teresa Bailey  

This issue of the journal brings together a number of interesting and informative contributions which explore new ground in areas that continue to be preoccupying for child psychotherapists.

The first three articles form a collection devoted to work with autistic children and adolescents. Although the emphasis of each article is different, they are all fine examples of clinicians working to connect with their patients to diminish mindless seclusion and adhesive ways of relating.

Amir’s article is of considerable theoretical interest, as she uses the musical concept of the organ point to consider how autistic syntax transforms normal multi-dimensional linguistic potential into something one-dimensional, repetitive and stripped of emotional range. Amir suggests that this autistic syntax blocks out the possibility of the presence and complexity of human characteristics of the self and the other. The other becomes the means by which the hole (created by the absence of the other as a psychological object) is plugged by their concrete presence. She argues that this results in the impossibility of a real dialogue as the language of the other is affected and inhibited by this autistic syntactic functioning. Repetitiveness removes the possibility that anything new can be allowed. This is an interesting look at the comparison of language and music in all their layers and how language can be rendered flat and devoid of creativity within relationships through autistic syntax.

The next two articles are primarily accounts of psychotherapy with autistic patients: Spoladore’s intensive work with a young child and Holloway’s contrasting experiences of working with two adolescents. Spoladore’s article includes a review of the literature on trauma, which seemed to be a precipitating aspect of the aetiology of her young patient’s autistic symptoms. Helping young Serge towards a more adaptive way of managing separation and loss is honestly and sensitively informed by the therapist’s parallel experience of personal loss. Spoladore’s patient had the benefit of intensive help at a young age when developmental opportunity is at its most favourable. Holloway in the next article argues that the onset of adolescence with its associated normal processes of separation–individuation provides another developmental opportunity to drive processes of emerging from autism. He explores difficulties in tolerating the separateness of others and attendant potential loss in clinical work with two adolescent boys. The striking contrast between their capacity to engage in psychotherapy as they grapple with similar issues is explored with sensitive tolerance by the author.

It is a privilege to comment on this session and on the work of a skilled therapist in his treatment of Rebecca. The therapist vividly conveys the session, including his own internal shifts and the patient’s movement between her different states of mind, or what I refer to as self-states.

In the previous session, Rebecca reported that she had recently cut herself using a set of antique razors bought for her by her father. Hearing this in the context of Rebecca’s history, I thought of the ‘family secret’ regarding her father’s mental health issues that had been disclosed by her older siblings. Why would he buy her antique razors?

Clinical commentary by Tessa Baradon, manager of the Parent Infant Project at the Anna Freud Centre

Tessa Baradon

Tessa Baradon

Anna Freud Centre 12 Maresfield Gardens
London
NW3 5SU
UK

Tessa Baradon  

This is a sensitive piece of work with a very young and vulnerable mother and her very young baby. Reading the background, the list of risk factors for the mother is long – she 230 is a teenage parent, rejected by her parents, with a history of attachment problems, for whom the conception of this child was a shocking mystery. The risk factors for the eight-week-old baby are also mounting – an immature and depressed mother, two losses of caregivers (mother and youth club leader) and at least some indications of possible emotional neglect (for example, mother is used to leaving her in her car seat).

Yet it is already evident that this young mother and baby have considerable strengths too. They are a responsive dyad – to each other and to the therapist’s holding. They are also capable of facing the pain entailed in the work that is to be done. This is a critical element in our psychoanalytic work and in work with mothers and infants; the mother’s wish to give positive life forces to her infant can be a strong ally for the therapist. The therapist, here, captures this beautifully: “your mummy loves you very much but is so little herself she finds it hard to know how to be a mummy.” The tone of the session indicates that the therapist – in only the third session – is already positively engaged with them.

The therapeutic process that unfolds follows an inner logic so that the development of trust, insight and tentative behavioural change takes place. The therapist conveys in words and in her manner a deep empathy and understanding of the mother’s predicament and how it may impact on the baby. This provides the holding framework within which emotional work can take place. Part of the psychological work is to transform confusion and inchoate pain into a narrative of meaning, a story of their intergenerational togetherness. Persecutory rage also finds its place in the construction of meaning through understanding of the transference. Following the therapist’s containment, mother finds ego strengths in herself (the nights are not so bad really) and is more able to attend to the emotions of her baby. Within the therapeutic encounter, there has been a sense of continuity from the past session, through to the sense of movement and rhythm in the here and now of this particular session – back and forward and yet with a beginning, middle and end – and on to a preparation for the next session.

The maternal lineage: identification, desire and transgenerational issues

Marilyn Lawrence

Marilyn Lawrence

120 Belsize Lane
London

Marilyn Lawrence  

, edited by Paola Mariotti, Hove, Routledge, 2012, 440 pp., £95 (hardback), ISBN 978-0-415-68164-3, £26.99 (paperback), ISBN 978-0-415-68165-0

This is an important book, bringing together a diverse range of papers in the psychoanalytic tradition from around the world. The topic is what the editor, Paola Mariotti, terms ‘maternality’. It is an awkward term and yet I think a necessary one. The editor quotes the OED definition as ‘the quality or condition of being maternal’ and she uses it to describe states of body and mind relating to being a mother. It seems a pity that we have to invent a word like maternality when we have the lovely, traditional word, ‘motherliness’. But this word seems to have become so affectively coloured as to make it unusable in a ‘scientific’ context. Something to think about.

The book is divided into three sections – ‘Mothering in body and mind’, ‘Subfertility and reproductive technologies’, ‘When not all goes well’ – with 14 papers in all. The authors include old favourites from Selma Fraiberg, Dinora Pines and Donald Winnicott as well as more recent contributions. The editor has chosen to focus principally on the issues of conception and pregnancy and the early days of motherhood. Unsurprisingly, the relationship of mother and daughter is one of the central themes. The questions posed on the back cover convey a sense of what the book is about, ‘Why do women want to have babies?’ ‘How does one learn to be a mother?’ ‘Does having babies have anything to do with sex?’ The majority of the papers in the book are previously published in journals, as one would expect. However, a number are in lesser known journals and the majority I had never read before, so the editor has done a very good piece of research in finding and drawing them together. There are a couple of papers which I think are original and one of them, by Dana Birksted-Breen, is a really helpful addition to the literature, looking at ways in which pregnant woman can (and cannot) make use of analysis at this pivotal period of their development. It is clinically very helpful and will personally resonate with analysts who are mothers.

Editorial

Teresa Bailey and Kate Stratton

Kate Stratton

Kate Stratton  

This last issue of the Journal for 2013 is a great tribute to the changes in our thinking and our application of psychoanalytic theory in the clinical work that now takes place in so many different settings and with an increasingly wide range of patients and professionals. 2013 marks the 50th anniversary of the Journal and we are pleased to include a rich edition with articles that reflect our development as a profession and our response to a changing world. We have papers on the experience of making a grant application for research, something that may well be of help to many of us who may face the prospect of such an undertaking before too long. There are papers on consultation in schools, on working with dissociative disorder in children, on how art can help us find a way to manage the many and increasing demands of our work and how film can be used in a wonderfully imaginative way to teach the concepts of psychoanalysis.

Elizabeth Edginton’s thought-provoking paper, presented at this year’s ACP conference, is a candid and lively account of the author’s experience of writing a National Institute of Health Research grant application for a randomised controlled trial feasibility study. Edginton usefully takes the reader through the key stages involved in developing the proposal, from the conceiving of the research project to the final elaboration of a written manual of the intervention to be tested. What brings the paper alive, however, are the author’s own unconscious-made-conscious associations to the process and her reflections on moving between the dual identities of clinician and researcher. Using a wide range of literary, cultural and psychoanalytic references, she poses a series of thought-provoking questions: does involvement in outcome research, as an individual, as an organisation and as a profession, ‘interrupt the clinical dyad’ of our more intimate case study research in a way that stirs up our most primitive Oedipal anxieties? What are the links between research and mourning? Do child psychotherapists need to make better use of our paternal function in order to free up our epistemophilic impulses and develop a more widely shared ‘research culture’? The article is a valuable contribution to the growing field of literature closing ‘the gap’ between practice and research and makes a powerful argument for research both as a creative activity and an essential partner to clinical work.

As previous clinical commentators have noted, it is a privilege to be able to read and think about a colleague’s work. In this context, without the benefits or protections (for both parties) afforded by a live conversation, making comments carries a particular duty of care.

Following the brief but regrettably familiar family history, I wondered whether Eve was separated from her siblings when in foster care due to sibling conflict and, if so, how the aggression was understood by the adults, and how the move was experienced and understood by Eve? Her initial indiscriminate and unfocussed behaviour in school made me think about Eve’s apparent lack of an available maternal object to provide not only individual nurture and containment, but also a gathering, organising and modulating capacity, perhaps akin to the paternal function of a nipple. This is, I think, also observable in the clinical work described. In the school group, Eve seems to have become quickly lost, overwhelmed, and perhaps frightened. Perhaps she was driven to a frantic searching for her lost sibling group, trying to locate them and herself with them, externally in the school group, and internally in her rather disorganised mind.

Notwithstanding the benefit of the assessing therapist’s experience with Eve, and the foreknowledge that this would be a complex girl to see individually, it is clear that the current child psychotherapist would require fortitude, creativity, and a good capacity to tolerant uncertainty. Eve’s frequent excursions out of the therapy room, walking away from what is on offer with the therapist, and the dropping of him/her in favour of another, expose the therapist to repeated experiences of being turned away from, and potentially shamed, in the public arena of the clinic. This could be thought about as arising in the realm of the transference. The therapist is clearly very committed and feels affection for Eve. It is also inevitable that a therapist in this position would, at times, feel very frustrated and annoyed with all the comings and goings, being picked up and dropped, and the exposure of the relationship and their work together.

Out of the mainstream: helping the children of parents with a mental illness

Gabrielle Crockatt

Gabrielle Crockatt

London
NW6 6LL
UK

Gabrielle Crockatt   *Email: gcrockatt@waitrose.com

In their seminal book Family Matters, editors Peter Reder, Mike McClure and Anthony Jolley (2000) made the case for joined up thinking regarding the mental health needs of children, young people and adults. They issued a challenge to those planning and providing mental health services, saying, ‘… creative initiatives could be conceived and implemented … These initiatives would recognise that, when one person presents with psychological problems, each other member of their family matters.’

Out of the Mainstream describes one such creative response. It is a description of the service developed in Tower Hamlets to address the needs of children whose parents suffered from mental illness. The book is edited, and a number of chapters are written, by Rosemary Loshak, the co-ordinator of the project; other professionals associated with the service have also contributed chapters. It is divided into three parts. The first sets out the issues to be addressed, the second describes the service that was developed in response to these issues and the third gives some of the backdrop to the project – the safety-net of other services and agencies within which it was able to operate.

Part One has two main themes – the situation in which these children and their families find themselves and the need for agencies to work together to meet the complexity of their needs. One myth that is quickly dispelled is that of ‘not burdening children with knowledge about their parent’s illness’. A chapter entitled, ‘What children say’ clearly shows that children know only too well from their daily experience that their parents are not alright. What they desperately need is help to understand what is going on and to know that they are not alone. A further chapter looks at the impact on children of parental illness, in particular on their safety and development. Child psychotherapists would probably hope to pursue this particular issue in more depth, for example by reference to the work of Gianna Williams (1998) in helping adolescents who have been recipients of parental projections.

Winnicott’s children: independent psychoanalytic approaches with children and adolescents

Judith Edwards

Judith Edwards

London
W11 4B, W
UK

Judith Edwards   *Email: Judith@judithedwards.co.uk

This is an excellent book and also a timely one – or one might also say ‘about time’. Its title (taken from Lanyado’s paper of the same name in the Winnicott Centenary edition of this journal) has a double ring. Winnicott himself had no children; the children he treated in such an inspirational way are the forerunners of the children that Independent clinicians, also his children as it were, treat now. He founded no training school and maybe at least a part of the reason for this was that he did not wish to have ‘followers’ and to be didactic. He thought we should all find our own way, in decent-enough clinical practice, without being too burdened by ideas of ‘right’ and ‘wrong’. He just wanted to communicate his own ideas to people and let them take them on and run with them as they wished. In this sense, he certainly comes across as being relatively non-narcissistic as far as that can be said of any of us. As he says in ‘Primitive emotional development’:

I shall not first give an historical survey and show the development of my ideas from the theories of others, because my mind does not work that way. What happens is I gather this and that, here and there, settle down to clinical experience, form my own theories and then, last of all, interest myself in looking to see where I stole what. Perhaps this is as good a method as any.

(Winnicott, 1945: 145)

Indeed. There is a playfulness here and it reflects his view of the infant who ‘gathers this and that, here and there’. He remained firm in the view that any individual’s lived experience must form the basis for creating and maintaining (as far as is ever possible) a coherence for oneself and a sense of personal integrity. As a pluralist myself I have always been drawn to his approaches alongside others and above all have found them to be extremely workable, useful and exciting .The idea of being alive to the moment in the Winnicottian sense is to be as Ogden (2001: 235) said, ‘forever in the process of making things of one’s own, whether they be thoughts, feelings, bodily movements, perceptions, conversations or analytic papers’. This is what drew me to Being Alive as a title for a collection of papers published in 2002 (Edwards, 2002).

Conceiving change: lay accounts of the human change process

Tracy A. Knight and Alphons A. Richert

Journal of Psychotherapy Integration, American Psychological Association, 2012, Volume 22 (3): 229–54

Recent challenges to the traditional view of the human change process – one that places emphasis primarily upon therapists’ perspectives – have led to attempts better to understand clients’ views of personal change. Although much is known about therapists’ viewpoints of the change process, this narrow attitude neglects the clients’ important contributions to psychotherapy. Understanding and working within the clients’ theories of change has significant clinical and research implications. Eighteen co-participants – including college-age, adult and senior individuals – were interviewed. Interviews were analysed using an iterative process based upon grounded theory. Codings were developed from the co-participants’ narratives based on unanimous decisions and themes were then developed reflecting the type of story shared. Three types of stories emerged from the data: Adaptation, Personal Choice and Delimited Choice. Co-participants’ relative lack of focus on particulars of the change process was evident. In addition, the stories often did not include personal agency as central to the change process. Clients may not come to therapy with a clear and easily elicited theory of change; the understanding of change that guides working with the client may be truly co-created by client and therapist within the psychotherapeutic process.

Blurring practice–research boundaries using progress monitoring

Marilyn Fitzpatrick

Canadian Psychology, American Psychological Association, 2012, Volume 53 (2): 75–81

Progress monitoring (PM) consists of using standardised measures to follow client progress and give clinicians feedback about response to treatment. PM systems have shown great promise in helping therapists identify when clients are not progressing, which improves both retention and client outcomes, but only if therapists use them. This article traces the story of the author’s halting and sceptical adoption of PM and the questions that were raised along the way. Beginning at the point of seeing PM as a good thing for others, the author presents a series of questions that centre on the issue of how PM fits with a therapeutic philosophy that values conversation over numbers.

Teresa Bailey and Kate Stratton

Kate Stratton

Kate Stratton  

This general issue of the journal contains some fascinating papers. We start with an article using a case study to look at how an infant might experience a post-natally depressed mother. The next three papers describe the therapists’ attempts at drawing out their patients: one from three years of silence, one from debilitating autism and the third from the trauma of a family tragedy. The final paper describes a study in psychic change processes in suicidal adolescents.

Salomonsson’s very detailed paper goes a little way to countering the paucity of published case studies of postpartum depression (PND) and its effects on an infant’s experience of its mother. The awareness of the importance of good infant mental health is growing but more evidence to support the argument for providing early therapeutic interventions is needed. It would be good to see more of such case studies especially given the prevalence of PND. A case study is provided of a little girl initially in treatment alongside her mother and then on her own in therapy with the same psychotherapist. Taking account of the child’s symptoms of restlessness, her longing for the breast, sleep difficulties and a fear of holes and ghosts, the author posits a psychoanalytic model of how a baby might experience a depressed mother. He suggests that babies of depressed mothers may not react to the depression itself but to the resulting disrupted containment, arousing overwhelming fears and the need for powerful emotional defences. It is a fascinating description of parent–infant work and how the therapist came to decide on moving the child into individual work. There is a great range of useful theoretical references.

Anagnostaki’s paper describes three years of silence in the intensive treatment of a pre-adolescent girl who had been diagnosed with ‘major depression’. The author examines the meaning of silence in the therapeutic context, something many of us have struggled with at times. Anagnostaki considers how the therapeutic environment can provide sufficient containment and psychic safety for patients so that they are able to take the opportunity to regress to a pre-verbal state. In this case, the long silence facilitated the growth of a more ‘mature “verbal” object’ relationship. Perhaps not enough is written about the silence we are often confronted with in the consulting room and how uncomfortable it can be for the therapist struggling to make sense of it. The author explores how she faced the repeated, seemingly endless challenges in this period of the therapy and eventually managed to find some meaning in the silence of her young patient.

Cortisol regulation in 12-month-old human infants: associations with the infants’ early history of breastfeeding and co-sleeping

Roseriet Beijers, J., Marianne Riksen-Walraven and Carolina de Weerth

Stress, Taylor & Francis, 2012, Early Online, DOI: 10.3109/10253890.2012.742057, 1–11

It is suggested that experiences during early life affect the physiological systems underlying stress responses, including the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis (HPA axis). While stressful early experiences have been associated with dysregulated HPA-axis functioning, positive early experiences, i.e. high quality maternal caregiving, contribute to more optimal HPA-axis functioning. Influences of other early caregiving factors, however, are less well documented. The goal of this study was to examine whether breastfeeding and co-sleeping during the first six months of life were associated with infant cortisol regulation, i.e. cortisol reactivity and recovery, to a stressor at 12 months of age. Participants were 193 infants and their mothers. Information on breastfeeding and co-sleeping was collected using weekly and daily sleep diaries, respectively, for the first six months of life. Co-sleeping was defined as sleeping in the parents’ bed or sleeping in the parents’ room. At 12 months of age, infants were subjected to a psychological stressor [Strange Situation Procedure (SSP); Ainsworth et al., 1978]. Salivary cortisol was measured pre stressor and at 25, 40 and 60 min post stressor to measure reactivity and recovery. Regression analyses showed that after controlling for maternal sensitivity, infant attachment status, feeding and sleeping arrangements at 12 months of age and other confounders, more weeks of co-sleeping predicted lower infant cortisol reactivity to the SSP. Also, more weeks of breastfeeding predicted quicker cortisol recovery. These results indicate that an early history of co-sleeping and breastfeeding contribute positively to cortisol regulation in 12-month-olds.

There is much said and left unsaid about Eve's life. We are given a summary of the main facts but there are many questions left to wonder about and this is probably the case for Eve and her adoptive mother too. I wanted to ask the therapist more about Eve’s history and present life but was reminded of how the experience of not knowing is such a pervading feature of the adopted child’s internal world. 357 How do you relax, grow and make the most of what’s available in the present when fundamental markers of life remain mysterious and are not known for various reasons?

Eve’s adoption at six years of age is very late and given the significant level of placement breakdown at this stage, we might think that Eve and her mother are doing well to remain together. The referral was made not long after Eve was placed for adoption and it is clear from the information given that Eve’s development has been significantly compromised. The assessment questions whether she will be able to manage individual work because of her reactiveness and inability to stay in the room, and it is decided that these two issues will become the focus of the therapy. This decision raises pertinent questions about what is the most effective intervention we can make in a situation like this. At times there can be a lot of pressure to work with children individually and this may well be the best intervention, however, I think there is a strong case to be made for working with adoptive children and their parents together. We know that Eve’s attachment patterns tend to be disorganised and she is highly anxious about separation; having her mother in the room, at least for the first phase of treatment, would offer the opportunity to work with both parties on these issues as they unfold in the session. A clinician trained in observation can be enormously helpful in enabling adoptive parents to notice, understand and feel less persecuted by some of the confusing behaviour they have to manage on a daily basis, often on their own.

Clinical material

Background

Eve is one of five children who were all taken into care following a history of domestic violence, physical abuse and neglect. Eve’s mother is physically well although she suffers from depression. No information is known about Eve’s birth father. Until her removal at the age of four and half, Eve lived with her mother and stepfather and four other siblings: three younger and one older than she was. Eve was born at term, a good weight, with no neonatal problems. She has remained physically well and achieved her developmental milestones with respect to gross and fine motor skills, but there were some concerns about Eve’s language, social and emotional development. Her speech was slow to develop. At three years of age, Eve was noted to have bruising on her face and body. Eve was reviewed again a few months later when she sustained other scratches and bruises on her body and face. This led to a Child Protection investigation and her removal from home.

Eve’s first placement was with two of her siblings. This lasted only 10 months. Eve formed a close relationship to her foster carer but had to move to a second placement to separate her from her siblings. She lived in this second placement for 11 months. She was then placed with her then prospective adoptive mother, a single adopter, at the age of six. She started to attend a local mainstream primary school in Year One where she displayed indiscriminate behaviour and was described as difficult to control and overly friendly to strangers. In the classroom, she had difficulties managing in group situations as well as keeping focused on tasks required of her. Classroom support needed to be funded for her.

Eve’s referral came to our team via her GP. Because of her reactiveness and inability to stay in the room without the presence of her mother during the sessions, the therapist who assessed her had doubts as to whether Eve would be able to work in a one-to-one psychoanalytic setting. The decision was made, however, to offer Eve once weekly sessions with me as her therapist on the basis that her reactiveness and inability to stay separate would be the focus of the work in the room with her. Eve is now 10 years old. We have been working together for two and half years. Mum is being seen by one of my colleagues for parent work.

Rebecca Bergese is a child psychotherapist working in London in private practice and teaching on Tavistock courses in London, Belfast and Florence. She is also an artist regularly showing her work in group and solo shows across the UK. She writes commentaries and short articles on contemporary art and is interested in researching mistakes.

Elizabeth Edginton is Research and Development Lead at the Northern School of Child and Adolescent Psychotherapy, and also works in CAMHS. She trained at the Birmingham Trust for Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy, and was formerly a university lecturer in Cultural Studies.

Angela Evans is a Tavistock-trained child and adolescent psychotherapist working in a specialist Looked After Children team within a CAMHS service in Sussex, and in private practice. Prior to this, she worked for 20 years in teaching, and specialised in working with children with special educational needs, including posts as a Special Educational Needs Co-ordinator for primary schools. She trains foster carers and social workers, and consults to Fostering teams in Children’s Services. She has a particular interest in attachment theory, and in applied psychoanalytic thinking to networks dealing with challenging children and families.

Carolyn Hart is a child and adolescent psychotherapist who works in a specialist CAMH team for looked after children in Sheffield. She has a particular interest in integrating findings from biology and neuroscience into her work with children who have suffered early relational trauma and its consequences.

Sue Kegerreis is a child and adolescent psychotherapist and adult psychotherapist. She is Director of the Centre for Psychoanalytic Studies at the University of Essex and has taught on a wide range of professional and academic courses. As a clinician she has practised in school, hospital and CAMHS settings and in private practice. She is author of Psychodynamic Counselling with Children and Adolescents: An Introduction (Palgrave Macmillan, 2010) and has published widely in professional journals. She is managing editor of Psychodynamic Practice.

Clinical commentary by Sara Rance, Consultant Child & Adolescent Psychotherapist, Newham CAMHS

On first reading this account of such a young mother coming into therapy with her two-month-old baby girl, my emotional responses ranged from foreboding to righteous indignation and a desire to rescue both mother and baby. The worker faces a daunting task, both in the direct therapy with the mother and infant and in the crucial work with the professional network. My countertransference feelings also relate to the wider social context in which this difficult work is taking place. There is no shortage of outraged finger wagging at professionals from journalists, civil servants, politicians and members of the public when serious harm befalls an infant or young child through abuse or neglect. The spectre of castigation hovers above us and external as well as internal pressures restrict the potential for unhurried reflection on the work. Like this young mother, we as professionals can feel constantly monitored and fear making a wrong move, yet we need a degree of freedom to take risk in the therapeutic work if development is to occur.

There are different perils in commenting on a snapshot of past clinical work: information is limited and there is no dialogue with the therapist. I miss details such as the gender of the therapist and something of the physical appearance of mother and baby. But even at one remove I feel a pressure to get it ‘right’, to alleviate the discomforting anxiety of being unsure – about what is unfolding moment by moment in the session and about whether this mother is capable of providing what her baby needs from her. In place of the position of certainty, different perspectives need to emerge – seeing the baby from the mother’s point of view and the mother from the baby’s point of view and both from the point of view of members of the professional network who may be in conflict with each other about what is in the best interests of mother and baby. With this in mind it is helpful that both baby and mother have their own social worker – good practice that, in my experience, is not always followed.

Clinical commentary: Clinical material


 

Clinical Commentary

Background

Rebecca is a 19-year-old referred to our clinic for intensive psychotherapy after a private assessment by an experienced clinician.

The initial private assessment was prompted by her mother who was deeply distressed and worried about Rebecca’s self-destructive behaviour. Rebecca had been abusing drugs and alcohol and self-harming since her mid-teens. Her alcohol abuse was such that she often blacked out, could not remember what had happened during her nights out drinking and had, on occasion, been in trouble with the police for abusive and violent behaviour towards people. Rebecca’s self-harming had been kept hidden from her mother until recently when her daughter came back home with her upper thighs covered in fine, superficial cuts. During the course of therapy, she told me she would also cut her upper arms but always kept her arms and legs covered so that no one could see the damage she had done to her body.

Rebecca is a very good-looking young woman, the classic English rose, very well spoken and well presented, clearly putting effort into the way she looks, dressed in trendy clothes with a slight but calculated bohemian edge to her overall image. She is musically talented and has aspirations as an actress.

She is the youngest of three and still living at home; her siblings are away at university but they often meet or spend time together. Her relationships with her two siblings appear to be quite complex; she often feels she cannot express her grievances or upsets in an open way with them; they are described as “domineering” and it seems as if between the three of them there is always some sort of argument or discord during which two siblings pair up against the third. Rebecca often feels that, being the youngest, she is scapegoated by the other two although she is not stuck in this position. Her parents separated when Rebecca was in her mid-teens, an event that deeply affected her and with which she is still struggling to come to terms. Rebecca feels very hard done by because she is the last child at home; she feels “responsible” for her mother’s well-being as she is convinced that if she were to leave home too, her mother would have a breakdown. At the same time, she speaks of enjoying having her mother all for herself.

Paula Conway  

There is a lot of information that we don’t have here, in particular an early developmental history that may tell us something about her mother’s state of mind and the support mother may or not have had during Rebecca’s infancy. We do know that she was the third child, that father has mental health problems and that the parents are separated. My hypothesis from this session is that for whatever reasons, Rebecca’s experience is of a maternal figure who projects back to Rebecca any disturbance that she attempts to project into her mother, rather than being able to contain her disturbance. Rebecca experiences this as a hostile rejection of her disturbed states of mind and this repeated experience leaves her with only omnipotent defences to manage very primitive states of intense anxiety and rage. This internal state can be seen in the description of her relationship with her siblings, where she feels she cannot express her grievances for fear she will be scapegoated with the disturbance pushed back into her.

First, though, what a very odd, even perverse, gift for her father to buy his daughter – a set of antique razors! I think it is a significant communication that in the previous session she tells the therapist she cut herself with father’s present. I would be curious to learn more about this. Does her father know of her cutting? Does she feel cut up by her father’s leaving? Is she furious her father has left her alone to deal with mother’s state of mind?

She begins this session by saying it was her birthday the day before and towards the end of the session she says she feels she is “coming out of it” (the depression) now her birthday is over. It seems that her birthday was really traumatic and in a roundabout way I felt the session was primarily an attempt to communicate just how disturbing she found her birthday and its implications.

The next communication is a rather bizarre description of how she has acclimatised herself to drinking again so she can get drunk on her birthday. The therapist is puzzled that she didn’t share any of this with her and planned it secretly, alone. The therapist says that Rebecca feels she has to do things by herself and wonders if this is connected to the missed previous sessions. Rebecca becomes distant and uninvolved. Although I agree with the therapist that Rebecca does feel she has to do things by herself and for herself, I don’t think she experiences this in a depressive way that can mourn the missed sessions or the therapist not being there for her birthday. I think rather this need to do things by herself comes from an omnipotent part of herself that has nothing to do with other people, and is contemptuous of other people. She is in charge of her drinking and her drunkenness. She is communicating here her need to bolster up ways of obliterating thinking by replacing it with an omnipotent lack of need for others, which she confirms by saying she didn’t want anyone around her on her birthday. She is angry that she doesn’t feel 20 only 18 (maybe more like 18 months or 18 weeks). She seems angry that she doesn’t feel equipped to manage the demands that life places on a 20-year-old. The therapist talks about her being in a different state of mind now from the beginning of the session, which I think does capture the rapidly fluctuating states of mind she experiences and this enables her to talk in a more genuinely depressive way about her anxieties about the changes she is facing, changes and expectations that are not under her omnipotent control.

Dana Amir is a clinical psychologist and a psychoanalyst from the Israeli Psychoanalytic Society. She works in private practice as a psychotherapist and psychoanalyst. Christopher Bonovitz is faculty and supervising analyst at the William Alanson White Institute and faculty analyst at New York University Postdoctoral Program in Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis and Stephen Mitchell Center For Relational Studies. He is associate editor of Psychoanalytic Dialogues, Journal of Contemporary Psychoanalysis and Journal of Infant, Child, and Adolescent Psychotherapy.

Paula Conway is a clinical psychologist and Tavistock trained psychoanalytic psychotherapist with 17 years experience working in clinical and community settings with children, young people, families and adults. Nicola Dugmore is an educational psychologist working as a psychoanalytic psychotherapist in private practice and in a community setting in Johannesburg, South Africa. She is currently completing her PhD in the area of mother–infant/child psychotherapy at the University of the Witwatersrand.

Viviane Green is programme manager of the MSc and Diploma in Psychodynamic Counselling with Children and Adolescents at Birkbeck College and an adult and child and adolescent psychoanalytic psychotherapist in private practice. Lisa is a teenage mother who became pregnant at the age of 15. She seemed very confused about how her baby was conceived, having had sex only once and not really knowing what had happened and how it had happened. When baby Anna was born, Lisa did not really have the chance to bond with her as the youth club leader, who did not have her own children, took over, getting up in the night, making bottles and soothing Anna to sleep. Angela Evans

Forest Row

RH18 5DS

Angela Evans  

SENCo, emotional and behavioural difficulties, Grounded Theory, countertransference, projective identification, containment

This paper draws on my doctoral research study based on consulting work with three primary school Special Educational Needs Co-ordinators (SENCos) that took place in 2008. The study examined the interactions that arose in the consultations with the SENCos and their staff. The findings that emerged from the application of Grounded Theory research methodology showed that the consultant, the SENCos and the children for whom they were responsible all felt on the edge of school life. SENCos and their staff were subject on a daily basis to powerful projections from children who were unable to tolerate difficult feelings and they were at risk of becoming identified with these feelings. The consultant in turn was the recipient of powerful projections from the SENCos. These complex dynamics of projective identification are examined in the study. The question of how SENCos and staff can better support children on the edge of exclusion with these unregulated feeling states is discussed. It is proposed that senior management teams and policy makers are essential in putting the SENCo role more at the centre of schools, both physically and in terms of how it is perceived. The need for access to a consultant who can help SENCos to understand and process extreme feelings is recommended as a way forward.

, by Elaine Arnold, London, Jessica Kingsley, 2012, 160 pp., £19.99, ISBN: 978-1-84310-992-1

It has been a real pleasure to read and to think about Elaine Arnold’s book in which she explores the interacting psychological, developmental, cultural, social and political themes in the lives of four generations of African Caribbean families. With roots in the 1950s and 1960s when, in the interests of economic survival, parents came to Britain leaving young children with extended family members in the Caribbean, sometimes for years, the book explores the detail of what occurred when parents and children were reunited and places these relational dynamics in their context.

Arnold includes the terrible and shameful historical details that predate the immigration of the ‘Windrush’ generation and much new information about the specifics of immigration from the Caribbean, alongside references to relevant research and a summary of her attachment-based research on both mothers and daughters separated as a result of these migrations. This gives readers in general, and particularly those working with African Caribbean families, a rich source of specific historical, cultural and psychological observations and analyses about the external world, the internal world and the intergenerational history of individuals we might encounter in a clinical, social or professional context. An extremely helpful and detailed counterbalance is thus provided for any tendency on the part of workers to stereotype either black foreigners or black British people and only see them through the lens of cultural difference thus avoiding key and specific experiences and the internal representations of these experiences. I especially appreciated Arnold’s focus on history and complexity and her capacity to think in a truly psychosocial way.

I believe I was asked to write this review because I am clinical director of a small charity working with young asylum seekers and refugees from all over the world, most of whom have been separated from their families through violence. Others live in families who have experienced significant losses of family members and community. These traumatic losses are difficult to mourn and significantly interfere with family life, relationships and individual development.

, edited by Nick Midgley and Ioanna Vrouva, Hove, Routledge, 2012, 240 pp., £80 (hardback), ISBN: 978-0-41560523-6, £22.99 (paperback), ISBN: 978-0-415-60525-0

In this interesting publication, Midgley and Vrouva begin by describing the aim of the book which is to provide an introduction to the theoretical concept of mentalization and to make a case for its relevance in clinical work with children, young people and their families.

Midgley and Vrouva explain that ‘the concept of mentalization is both a relatively new one and an extremely old one’. Mentalization is defined as a form of ‘imaginative mental activity’ involving the capacity to perceive and interpret human behaviour with regard to intentional mental states. The editors suggest that mentalizing involves the accurate perception of mental states that includes such elements as desires, needs, beliefs, feelings, reasons and goals. That mentalization is a fundamental aspect of what it is to be a human being has been put forward by a number of clinicians who also believe that mentalization plays a central role in the ability to regulate emotional states, in developing the capacity to reflect upon mental states of self and others and is a crucial factor in lending coherence to a sense of self. Midgley and Vrouva emphasise that mentalization is very much an applied science with roots not only in the theoretical domain but also developing from various aspects of clinical practice.

The book clearly demonstrates that mentalization-based treatment has become an evidence-based practice, primarily with regard to work with borderline personality disorder. However, the book promulgates that the application of mentalization-based approaches has increased to include different types of work with children, young people and families. Indeed its popularity has become such that community-based projects that have adopted mentalization-based thinking have developed to inform practice and thinking about children, young people and their families. A number of these projects are discussed in the book. The popularity of mentalization has not been limited to the UK. The book highlights how mentalization in its applied form has gained impetus in areas of mental health and social policy around the world thanks in part to the coherent way in which it synthesises a broad base of thinking about development, pathology and treatment. An advantage for those clinicians adopting mentalization-based treatments is the emphasis it places upon helping to inform existing ways of working; it is not seen as a replacement for the clinician’s training or existing experience. Midgley and Vrouva use the phrase ‘mentalization-enhancing interventions’, which can be useful additions or ‘refinements’ to most psychosocial forms of treatment. They add that: ‘This is because attending to mental states in oneself and others is a fundamental common factor inherent in any psychotherapeutic work’ (p. 2).

Judith Jackson

This book brings to life the extraordinary figure of Martha (Mattie) Harris (1919–87), and every contribution to this collection is a living testament to her dynamic and continuing influence on the developing field of psychoanalytic work with children and parents. She was a brilliant and unique teacher, much loved by several generations of child psychotherapists who were fortunate to be trained by her and she continues to live on inside them as an enabling and inspiring presence. I was one such young trainee in the late 1960s and feel touched and privileged to be asked to review this book as it evokes all my own memories of being ‘enabled and inspired’ by the richness of her teaching, her clinical insights, human wisdom and personal kindnesses to me.

It is not possible to do justice to all the varied accounts of her teaching or the many moving tributes and recollections of her generosity and motherliness to all her students, but what is so remarkable is that, quite separately, each writer brings out Mattie’s very special, perhaps even idiosyncratic personality so that even if you had never known her, her presence is splendidly vivid. We can picture her, a tall woman in her floral, self-made flowing dress, with heavy-lidded, almost sleepy and yet penetratingly attentive piercing grey-blue eyes, carrying and sometimes dropping files and papers, both flustered, verbally hesitant, even vulnerable and yet clear minded and confident, dealing with the moment and keeping everyone and everything in mind. As Margot Waddell writes, her style was less about conventional ‘knowledge’ than about wisdom. Above all she was a deeply humane person.

The book is divided into three sections: ‘In England and abroad’; ‘Clinical work and supervision’ and ‘Personal recollections’. There is, however, considerable overlapping between each of these. Her daughter, Meg Harris Williams, writes in the preface that Mattie had a concern that unless ideas could ‘travel and find their own form in other minds and places, they would disappear or fossilise’ and the book demonstrates very clearly how successful she was in exporting psychoanalytic ideas.

Louise Allnutt   *Email: lallnutt@tavi-port.nhs.uk

To approach the task of writing this review is rather daunting. A relative newcomer – very much at the beginning of a career in child psychotherapy – making notes and comments on the work of someone who has attended to the experience of beginnings and endings for the last 60 years or so seems rather at odds with the scope of the book. This is very much a life’s work and when the reviewer’s life experience goes little beyond the realms of chapter 10 (there are 13 chapters in all) then one should probably simply suggest to the readership that this book, along with life itself, just needs to be experienced. However, despite this clear discrepancy there is a great deal to say about this book and a good deal one can learn both from what it tells us and how these messages are delivered.

This book is written with seemingly effortless fluency. Turning the pages comes with equal ease, aided by the rhythm of a voice whose tone is deeply understanding at the same time as being alive to the world and gratefully optimistic. It is of course concerned with beginnings and endings and there are several examples embedded within its chronological structure as well as the personal narratives that run throughout. However, for me the binding thread of the book is a motif that emerges at various points along the way and draws our attention to how these beginnings and endings are ‘experienced’. As Isca writes, ‘at every turn, as Bion (1962) says, we have to choose whether to avoid emotional pain or to face it; to live with lies, or to live with truth, which he calls “the food that nourishes the mind”’ (11).

The choice either to face our fears or avoid them sounds oddly straightforward and yet the optimism with which this book is written appears to confirm that despite all of our unconscious and conscious resistances, to stand face to face with true experience and its emotional ramifications, is nevertheless possible. And more than this, to do so, while painful, leads to greater fulfilment. A Kleinian model underpins the core observations and understanding of the ‘almost universal avoidance of endings’ (11), but our attention is also drawn to a spiritual dimension in human experience that ultimately makes growth possible. An inner capacity to ‘remain open to and moved by the wonder of life in what we see and hear and intuitively sense, an awareness of the preciousness of life despite the destructive forces without and within ourselves’ (13). Drawing on a wealth of experience in infant observation Wittenberg points out that this capacity is naturally drawn from our earliest experiences as infants and to some degree granted to us constitutionally. With reference to the transitional moments in our emotional and social development, she reminds us that we also have the opportunity to develop such a capacity in relationships with our teacher, partners and children and when it feels too overwhelming, our analysts and therapists.

The grandmaternal transference in parent–infant/child psychotherapy

Nicola Dugmore

Nicola Dugmore

94 Henrietta Road, Norwood 2192
Johannesburg, South Africa

Nicola Dugmore  

Parent–child psychotherapy, parent–infant psychotherapy, maternal grandmother, motherhood constellation, grandmaternal transference

The psychic significance of the figure of the grandmother in psychodynamic psychotherapy has received scant attention. This paper develops the concept of the ‘grandmaternal transference’ in parent–infant psychotherapy and explores its identification, its possible functions and its therapeutic significance. The grandmaternal transference has special relevance to parent–infant psychotherapy since the grandmother often represents both the mother’s mother and the child’s grandmother and offers a unique third position between mother and child. Three clinical vignettes illustrate how the grandmaternal transference may operate in this third position. In the first vignette, the therapist becomes in the transference a containing grandmother thereby facilitating maternal containment. In the second case, the therapist may be experienced as a differentiating grandmother able to help mother and infant with separation and individuation. In the third one, the therapist is transferentially experienced as a paternal grandmother who acts as a pseudo-father able to embody the paternal function. In each of these positions, the transference and countertransference – whether positive or negative – require that the therapist responds to rather than enacts the grandmaternal role. The three configurations of the grandmaternal transference have different clinical manifestations and offer different therapeutic ports of entry.

This paper retraces the steps in the recovery of a capacity for thinking in a boy who was five at the time his mother was tragically murdered by his father and almost 11 years old when he began psychoanalytic psychotherapy. It describes the emotional and technical difficulties of working psychotherapeutically when there seemed to be neither the thoughts nor the words with which to engage and experience the mental pain that lay frozen behind his eyes. I describe in detail the slow unfolding of a process in which Michael appeared to be quite literally rebuilding the structure and internal space of his mind in his play and in the transference. He needed to repair his internal thinking apparatus and recover his capacity for containment before he could house his own traumatic feelings and thoughts and think about them with me. The commensal relationship of container and contained grew out of tolerating unbearable amounts of doubt (W.R. Bion, Learning from Experience, London: Heinemann, 1962) in the transference–countertransference. This was only possible through the triangular space provided by the presence of an analyst and a supervisor in my mind and the generous support provided by colleagues and Michael’s dedicated grandparents.

Psychic processes underlying suicidal behaviours during adolescence and their evolution are explored. A longitudinal study was conducted of thirty adolescent patients hospitalised following a suicide attempt. Clinical interviews were used combined with the Rorschach Test and the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) a few days after the suicide attempt and one year later. Results initially showed common forms of psychic adjustment: melancholic identifications were linked to an excessive dependence on objects. One year later, these forms of psychic adjustment changed: for many adolescents, the melancholic identifications shifted and self-image improved. The emergence of representations of murder fantasies immediately after the suicidal behaviour allowed a possible transformation of violence into symbolisation. A case study illustrates these psychic changes.

Despite the high prevalence of postnatal depression (PND) and the focus in psychoanalytic theory on the importance of the infant’s primary relationship with the mother, few case studies have been published. This applies to PND mothers in psychoanalysis and mother–infant dyads in psychotherapy. A case of a girl in treatment from 16 to 40 months of age is presented in three clinical vignettes. She was first in treatment with mother and then continued on her own in regular child analysis. Her main symptoms were restlessness and craving for the breast, later followed by a fear of holes and a phobia of ghosts combined with difficulties falling asleep. Based on this case, a psychoanalytic model is suggested of how the infant might experience being with the PND mother. The author suggests that infants of such mothers do not react to their depression per se but to a faltering containment. This leaves the baby with frightening emotions. The experience of insufficient containment may be represented in different ways such as, in this case, a fear of holes and voids and, in the next step, a phobia erected in defence of this fear.

Autism, auto sensuousness, sensation-dominated state

This paper is the story of the 12-year treatment of a very bright and very impaired adolescent male encapsulated in autistic retreat. It is also the story of the author’s discovery of the work of Frances Tustin and the light that this shed on the author’s understanding of her patient. The author explains how Tustin’s ideas about autistic processes helped her to understand her patient’s sensory distress and his debilitating withdrawal from all human contact. She also explains her efforts to maintain contact with him and gradually to draw him back into a relationship with his family and members of his community. His willingness to forge a relationship with the author and his own desire to understand himself were great aids in his healing.

I finished reading the clinical material and noticed how irritated I had come to feel. When I re-read it, my discomfort grew. I felt unusually critical. Given that the actual material does not warrant such a response, what was going on within me? Who was I identifying with such that I wanted to reject the material in a critical way? It was disconcerting: after all, a thoughtful therapist had described a third session with a 15-year-old mother and her two-month-old baby, yet I felt judgmental and, at first, critical of her potentially creative questions, interpretations and embodied actions. There are many possibilities for my experience, several of which could be simultaneously relevant. What follows is one hypothesis.

A moment of authentic expression seemed to occur some time into the session when mother Lisa could express her unnamed but powerfully felt fury at feeling judged and restricted. She mentioned not being allowed to take baby Anna out on her own yet; or being allowed to have any time on her own. The theme of ‘not being allowed …’ filled the exchange. I bristled with frustration when I considered the restrictions Lisa was expected to adhere to and asked myself what evidence Social Care had to justify preventing a young mother, who had not harmed her baby, to go for a walk on her own with her baby, or have some time with friends without her baby? With many teenage mothers, a grandmother or aunt would naturally offer to help for a few hours to give the mother a bit of space. There is often an inherent understanding in the grandparent that adolescence and full-time responsibility for the survival of a baby create understandable tensions and help is offered to support the adolescent negotiate her conflicting wishes. This was not allowed for mother Lisa and so the question is raised as to how the network of professionals involved in the case might be acting into Lisa’s history and her family dynamics?

Lisa’s father’s harsh rejection of his daughter crashed into my thoughts and an uncomfortable insight started to emerge. Was I in identification with him? This man who ‘did not want Lisa to remain in the house’? Mother Lisa’s crime seemed to have been to face her father with her sexuality and fecundity all at once. His response was to become powerfully rejecting, castrating the young man who dared impregnate his daughter and shaming her for exploring her sexual life. Efficacy of family-based treatment for adolescents with eating disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis

Jennifer Couturier, Melissa Kimber & Peter Szatmari

International Journal of Eating Disorders, Wiley, 2012, Volume 46 (1): 3–11

Objective: To systematically review and quantitatively evaluate the efficacy of Family-Based Treatment (FBT) compared with individual treatment among adolescents with eating disorders. Method: The literature was reviewed using the MEDLINE search terms ‘family therapy AND Anorexia Nervosa,’ and ‘family therapy AND Bulimia Nervosa’. This produced 12 randomised controlled trials involving adolescents with eating disorders and family therapy which were reviewed carefully for several inclusion criteria including: allocation concealment, intent-to-treat analysis, assessor blinding, behavioural family therapy compared with an individual therapy and adolescent age group. References from these articles were searched. Only three studies met these strict inclusion criteria for meta-analysis. A random effects model and odds ratio was used for meta-analysis, looking at ‘remission’ as the outcome of choice. Results: When combined in a meta-analysis, end of treatment data indicated that FBT was not significantly different from individual treatment (z=1.62, p=0.11). However, when follow-up data from 6 to 12 months were analysed, FBT was superior to individual treatment (z=2.94, p< 0.003), and heterogeneity was not significant (p=0.59). Discussion: Although FBT does not appear to be superior to individual treatment at end of treatment, there appear to be significant benefits at 6–12-month follow-up for adolescents suffering from eating disorders.

A substantive and methodological review of family-based treatment for eating disorders: the last 25 years of research

Karly J. Downs & Adrian J. Blow

Journal of Family Therapy, Blackwell, 2013, Volume 35 (Suppl. 1): 3–28

This article provides a substantive and methodological review of all research studies published in the last 25 years that have evaluated a family-based intervention as a central component in the treatment of eating disorders (specifically anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa). While in the past 25 years there has been an increase in research exploring the efficacy of family therapy in the treatment of eating disorders, there has not been a comprehensive review of all these studies. Rather, reports of studies of family therapy and eating disorders are scattered in a wide range of journals and disciplines. Here we summarise the findings, provide a critique of the methodologies used, discuss methodological challenges and suggest next steps for research and clinical practice.

Adhesive unity, adolescence, chuntering, high-functioning autism, loss, mourning, separation

Aspects are outlined of the psychotherapy of two adolescents who were starting to emerge from a previous state of chronic (though high-functioning) autism. A central theme is the difficulty these adolescents had in tolerating the separateness of others (and thus the possibility that others could be lost) and at the same time being unable to remain content with a state of autistic adhesive unity with the other. This contribution is an attempt to build on the work of a number of highly creative psychoanalytic pioneers in the understanding of autistic children and adolescents and their application to these children of ideas involving symbiotic at-one-ness and fears of psychic separateness. The influences of Frances Tustin, Anne Alvarez, Thomas Ogden and Susan Reid are particularly key.

This paper is presented as a potential teaching resource for those starting out in their psychoanalytic understanding, whether aiming at clinical work or the academic study of psychoanalytic ideas. Some central ideas from Freud and Klein are illustrated and illuminated in an accessible way using the Disney film The Lion King. Dana Amir

Dana Amir

Shderot Hanassi 54

Dana Amir  

Autism, primary mental states, trauma, autistic syntax, psychic organ point, autistic dyad, reclamation of psychic polyphony

This paper deals with autistic syntax and its expressions both in the fully fledged autistic structure and in the autistic zones of other personality structures. The musical notion of the organ point serves as a point of departure in an attempt to describe how autistic syntax transforms what was meant to constitute the substrate for linguistic polyphony into a one-dimensional, repetitive score, devoid of emotional volume. Autistic syntax denies the recognition of the human characteristics of both self and other, turning the other into an autistic object, which blocks, with his or her concrete presence, the hole created by his or her own absence as a psychological subject. The resulting discourse either imprints its forms on the other’s language or rubs against its surface, but never creates a living dialogue. Within the autistic discourse, repetitiveness replaces cross-fertilisation, thereby annihilating the ability to create or to allow anything new. The paper concludes with a discussion of Tustin’s notion of ‘the function of the cross’ within the therapeutic process and its communicative expressions in language.

1This article illustrates a little boy’s journey from autistic-like symptoms into more adaptive ways of coping with trauma and separation. Drawing from the psychoanalytic literature on autism and trauma, it discusses how traumatic events in the first two years of life may cause a child to withdraw from social relationships and cause developmental delay. Using the case of a young child in intensive psychotherapy, the article considers his experience of separation and looming loss at an early age and also explores how the author’s concomitant bereavement impacted on the countertransference. In addition, the shifts in the young boy’s relationship to inanimate objects and particularly his attraction to rubber, is considered with reference to the psychoanalytic concepts of ‘autistic sensation’ and ‘transitional phenomena’. The author demonstrates how planning and preparing for the end of treatment was an essential part of the psychotherapy, helping the patient to develop resilience and to live through the experience of separation.

After reading this record of a session of clinical work, I was left with a number of thoughts and feelings. I was concerned about several aspects of Rebecca’s life and what seemed to me to be her fragile personality development. Rebecca appeared to be ‘emotionally homeless’ as if she has no base or sense of a reliable object and is not equipped, internally, for the uncertainties of life as she prepares to move into young adulthood.

98

I am concerned about Rebecca’s capacity to manage to live in a safe and ordinary way as she moves on with her life, away from home and her therapy. This leaves me with feelings of anxiety and sadness as I try to pull together my emotional and thinking responses to the clinical material.

I wonder about endings in therapy and how difficult these are for the child or young person we are seeing. I remember a seminar leader helpfully encouraging me to think aloud with the young person about what they might take with them from the experience of being in therapy with their therapist. Has Rebecca got an object that can take in and make sense of her experiences of her therapy? I am curious about the public external identity of Rebecca and the more private, internal identity and wonder about Rebecca’s struggle to bring these different aspects of herself together in a more integrated way.

The transition from childhood to adulthood is a complicated physical and emotional process and Rebecca does not appear to be as well prepared, equipped or supported, as many young people might need to be in order to manage these transitions.

One of the first things we are told about Rebecca is that she is ‘very good-looking – a classic English rose, very well spoken and well presented with a bohemian edge, a musical talent and aspirations to be an actress’. There is a sense that this is an idealised view of her and that, as a result of these external qualities, she might be envied and idealised by others but that, privately, she might need to ‘live in the skin of others’ as her own skin is not comfortable or containing enough for her. I wonder if she is really struggling to be herself, to find a role in her own drama of life.

The thinking heart: three levels of psychoanalytic therapy with disturbed children

Judy Shuttleworth

Judy Shuttleworth

69 Collingwood Avenue
London, N10 3EE
UK

Judy Shuttleworth  

, by Anne Alvarez, London, Routledge, 2012, 214 pp., £85 (hardback), £23.99 (paperback), ISBN: 978-0-415-55486-2 (hb), 978-0-415-55487-9 (pb)

This is an account of what that often empty bureaucratic phrase ‘life-long learning’ might really mean if pursued with diligence, intelligence and courage. It allows the reader to share in the fruits of a life time of learning and disciplined thinking. Anne Alvarez is now in a position to look back on different stages in her professional practice and the patients who challenged her. A committed psychoanalytic psychotherapist and, latterly, a clinician-researcher, Alvarez has always taken an imaginative and critical stance towards psychoanalytic theory, seeking to integrate different perspectives within psychoanalysis with the ideas that have been emerging from developmental psychology and neuroscience. Linked together, these perspectives on normal development and psychopathology helped her observe and think about the states of being she encountered in traumatised, withdrawn and autistic child patients, sustaining her in working with them over long periods. This book draws on clinical work, psychoanalytic theory, infant observation and infant research. It offers an account of psychoanalytic psychotherapy with children that is both inspiring and daunting.

Anne Alvarez has been so influential within child psychotherapy for so long that it is difficult to think back to a time when the ideas she is describing here had not yet emerged. From the 1970s, child psychotherapists in the UK were feeling an increasing need to develop their way of working in response to the range and severity of difficulties among the children and adolescents presenting in public clinics and private consulting rooms. Alvarez has given a large part of her professional life to thinking and writing about the particular needs of traumatised and autistic child patients and the demands they make of clinicians.

In this book, as in her other writing, she returns to her early clinical records to examine in detail what she came to see as errors and deficiencies in her understanding and in her clinical technique for communicating that understanding. By studying therapeutic failure she was able get closer to the experience of these patients and to find more direct ways to grasp, on their behalf, the raw felt qualities of what was happening to them so that they could begin, in time, to grasp and inhabit something of their own experience. Through this she came to the view that psychoanalytic technique has historically been focused on interpretations that were essentially explanatory, linking different aspects of psychic life together to gain an understanding of underlying patterns of motivation. What Alvarez felt many of her patients needed from her was something different – the persistence to gain the attention of a very withdrawn or despairing child and only then a very brief description of something that had happened, offered as a point of potential shared interest.

The following paper has grown out of a spoken presentation given to the annual conference of the ACP in June 2012. Beginning from ideas that have emerged from reading and experiencing the work of Bion, the presentation attempted to apply these ideas to some of the issues that face child psychotherapists working in publicly funded health services today, and to suggest that rather than truncate our clinical and professional thinking to meet the demands of shrinking budgets and evidence based practice, we should embrace our capacities for observation and ‘reverie’ not only within our clinical work, but in the professional activities beyond. Using brief discussion of the work of artists, the paper revives our knowledge of the unconscious mind’s potential for repair, often making creative developments out of forgotten resources in unnoticed spaces. In fact it is the forgotten, unnoticed and discarded that have the potential to be the richest resources in a time when more conventional resources are fading.
